lines.192: This chapter is long, but be at ease, Louise. Much of this chapter consists of examples that illustrate the ideas discussed here. Most of it is not difficult.
lines.194: There’s a good deal to know about verbs, including the matters of verb tenses and the related notions of the principal parts of verbs and the regular and irregular verbs.
lines.195: The good news is that you know much of this already. You’ve used the tenses and principal parts ever since you learned to talk. What may be new to you here are the terms that we apply to them and the way we organize them. So relax, Max.
lines.199: Tense? We don’t mean over-caffeinated verbs. We mean that, in the right context, verbs communicate that an action took place in the present, past, or future.
lines.200: English has four sets of tenses, and each set contains a present, a past, and a future tense, each with its own distinctions in refer- ence to time. Here we’ll examine briefly all four sets:
lines.202: The simple tenses: present, past, and future. The perfect tenses: present, past, and future.
lines.204: SIMPLE PRESENT: SIMPLE PAST: SIMPLE FUTURE:
lines.206: Today I phone my mother. Yesterday I phoned my mother. Tomorrow I will phone my mother.
lines.207: The simple progressive tenses: present, past, and future. The perfect progressive tenses: present, past, and future.
lines.211: These are the tenses we use most often:
lines.213: Notice that we seldom use the simple present in a sentence like “Today I phone my mother.” Instead, we use the simple past:
lines.215: Today I phoned my mother. Or we use the simple future,
lines.217: Today I will phone my mother.
lines.219: Or we use a tense that we’ll examine in a moment, the present progressive tense:
lines.221: I’m phoning my mother right now.
lines.222: But we’ll continue to use this somewhat unusual form in our examples of the simple present.
lines.224: Here are more examples of the simple tenses:
lines.226: SIMPLE PRESENT: SIMPLE PAST: SIMPLE FUTURE:
lines.228: Today I talk. Yesterday I talked. Tomorrow I will talk.
lines.230: SIMPLE PRESENT: SIMPLE PAST: SIMPLE FUTURE:
lines.232: SIMPLE PRESENT: SIMPLE PAST: SIMPLE FUTURE:
lines.234: Today I walk. Yesterday I walked. Tomorrow I will walk.
lines.236: Today I build. Yesterday I built. Tomorrow I will build.
lines.237: As these examples show, we create the simple present tense by using the simplest possible form of a verb. The simple present ends with -s in cases like these: he phones, he talks, he builds.
lines.239: For the great majority of English verbs, we create the simple past tense by adding -d (as in phoned) or -ed (as in talked, walked, or hunted) to the present form. In a few cases, we make the past by adding -t (as in built).
lines.240: With all verbs, we create the simple future tense by adding the auxiliary verb will to the simple present form.
lines.244: The perfect tenses are not called perfect because they’re flawless. (Only your grammar teacher is flawless.) They are called perfect because the perfect tenses describe actions that have already been completed (i.e., perfected) at some point in the past, present, or future.
lines.245: All the perfect tenses are based on a form of the main verb called the past participle, which in most verbs is identical to the form in the simple past tense. (We’ll see more of the past participle a bit later.)
lines.247: Verbs in the present perfect tense always add the auxiliary verb have (or has) to the past participle form. They refer to actions that were recently completed:
lines.249: I have called my mother today. She has called her mother today.
lines.250: Verbs in the past perfect tense always add the auxiliary had to the past participle form. They refer to actions completed at some point in the past:
lines.252: I had called my mother by noon yesterday.
lines.253: The future perfect tense, like the simple future tense, always begins with the auxiliary will, followed by have:
lines.254: By noon tomorrow I will have called my mother. Here are some examples:
lines.256: PRESENT PERFECT: PAST PERFECT: FUTURE PERFECT:
lines.258: PRESENT PERFECT: PAST PERFECT: FUTURE PERFECT:
lines.259: PRESENT PERFECT: PAST PERFECT: FUTURE PERFECT:
lines.262: As of yesterday, I had talked.
lines.263: By this time tomorrow I will have talked.
lines.266: As of yesterday, I had walked.
lines.267: By this time tomorrow I will have walked.
lines.270: As of yesterday, I had complained.
lines.271: By this time tomorrow I will have complained.
lines.272: If you compare the main verbs in these perfect tense sentences with the main verbs in the simple past sentences that we saw earlier, you’ll see that they are exactly the same words. This is a point that we’ll return to when we discuss regular and irregular verbs.
lines.274: THE SIMPLE PROGRESSIVE AND PERFECT PROGRESSIVE TENSES
lines.275: The simple progressive tenses refer to actions that have been in progress at a particular point in time. The main verbs in the progressive tenses always end in -ing, and they always take an auxiliary verb that is a form of the verb be.
lines.277: The future progressive tense always begins with the auxiliaries will be. Here are some examples:
lines.279: PRESENT PROGRESSIVE: PAST PROGRESSIVE: FUTURE PROGRESSIVE:
lines.281: PRESENT PROGRESSIVE: PAST PROGRESSIVE: FUTURE PROGRESSIVE:
lines.282: PRESENT PROGRESSIVE: PAST PROGRESSIVE: FUTURE PROGRESSIVE:
lines.284: Today I am phoning. Yesterday I was phoning. Tomorrow I will be phoning.
lines.286: Today I am hunting. Yesterday I was hunting. Tomorrow I will be hunting.
lines.288: Today I am griping. Yesterday I was griping. Tomorrow I will be griping.
lines.290: In the perfect progressive tenses, we describe actions that have been in progress but were completed (or will be completed) in the present, past, or future.
lines.291: The main verb is still an -ing form, and it always has two aux- iliaries: a form of have followed by been. In fact, all the auxiliaries in all tenses of the perfect progressive are perfect tenses of the verb be. In the present perfect progress, the auxiliaries are have been or (with third-person singular subjects) has been. In the past, they are had been. And, of course, in the future perfect progressive, the auxiliaries are will have been.
lines.292: PRESENT PERFECT PROGRESSIVE: PAST PERFECT PROGRESSIVE: FUTURE PERFECT PROGRESSIVE:
lines.294: PRESENT PERFECT PROGRESSIVE: PAST PERFECT PROGRESSIVE: FUTURE PERFECT PROGRESSIVE:
lines.296: Today I have been phoning. Yesterday I had been phoning. By this time tomorrow I will have been phoning.
lines.298: Today I have been hunting. Yesterday I had been hunting. By this time tomorrow I will have been hunting.
lines.300: PRESENT PERFECT PROGRESSIVE: PAST PERFECT PROGRESSIVE: FUTURE PERFECT PROGRESSIVE:
lines.301: Today I have been grousing. Yesterday I had been grousing. By this time tomorrow I will have been grousing.
lines.304: Most English verbs have consistent verb forms that we use to create the tenses we’ve just examined. These are called regular verbs, which means that the form to create the past tense and the perfect tenses are the same. That is, in both the simple past tense and the perfect tenses, we add –d or -ed, or (in a few cases) add a final -t. No other change in spelling happens, as you’ll see in the table below.
lines.305: So we say that every verb (except some auxiliary verbs) has three principal parts: the present, the past, and the past participle (which is the form used with have for perfect tenses). These are usually presented in a table like this:
lines.315: I talked I have talked I hunted I have hunted I phoned I have phoned I built I have built
lines.317: All of these are regular verbs. The past and past participle are the same word.
lines.318: Notice the relatively new verb to phone. Newly-created English verbs are always regular: fax, faxed; text, texted; friend, friended. (But there is at least one exception: We hung out at the mall.)
lines.320: When we speak of a fourth principal part, it’s always the present participle, the -ing form used for progressive tenses: talking, hunting, phoning, building. And the -ing form is easy.
lines.323: Irregular verbs are less consistent in their past and past participle forms. Although English has fewer irregular verbs than regular, there are hundreds of them. Many are among the most commonly used verbs in English.
lines.329: I begin I break I bring I drink I drive I fly
lines.331: I freeze I know I ride
lines.336: I speak I swim I swing I take
lines.360: I have broken I have brought I have drunk
lines.364: I have known I have ridden I have rung
lines.367: I have spoken I have swum
lines.371: All of us make errors now and then with some of the irregular verbs, and it’s a good idea to identify those that give you the most trouble and study them. The table above gives you some of the most common irregulars, and you can find complete lists in many grammar books and on the Internet. A dictionary can always help you with specific verbs.
lines.373: One way to study irregulars is to group the verbs that are similar in their past and past participle forms, like this:
lines.376: I begin I drink I ring
lines.379: I break I freeze I speak
lines.381: I drive I ride I write
lines.388: I began I drank I rang
lines.391: I broke I froze I spoke
lines.393: I drove I rode I wrote
lines.399: I have begun I have drunk I have rung
lines.400: I have sunk I have swum
lines.402: I have broken I have frozen I have spoken
lines.404: I have driven I have ridden I have written
lines.406: I have flown I have known
lines.408: The following are verbs that you may also want to study. The verb dive is in fact regular:
lines.409: I dive I dived I have dived
lines.411: But dove, as a past and past participle, has become so common that it is now widely accepted.
lines.413: We might call the verb burst “super-regular”. It doesn’t change at all:
lines.415: Today I burst Yesterday I burst I have burst
lines.417: Other super-regular verbs include hit, set, and split.
lines.419: Shine is a peculiar case. Used as a transitive verb (which we’ll study soon), it’s regular: They have shined their trophies every month.
lines.421: They shine They shined They have shined
lines.422: As an intransitive verb (another term that’s coming up), it’s irregular: The sun has shone all day.
lines.424: It shines It shone It had shone
lines.426: The verb hang is also peculiar, taking different forms depending on its meaning. Imagine you’re in a dusty little town in the Old West, and you ask a gnarled old-timer, “Whatever happened to that grammar teacher?” And the old-timer answers,
lines.428: We’ve hanged that danged grammar teacher. He was all the time correctin’ us!
lines.429: But if you’re proudly displaying your framed diploma on the wall, you could say,
lines.432: There are six verbs (grouped in pairs below) that confuse us all at some point:
lines.434: I sit down. I lie down. I rise up.
lines.436: I set the books down. I lay the books down. I raise the books up.
lines.448: I have sat I have set
lines.452: I have risen I have raised
lines.462: In the left column, the verbs indicate the way you are positioning yourself. They are all irregular verbs. In the right column, the verbs indicate the way you are positioning the object (or anything else separate from yourself). They are all regular.
lines.464: It’s easy to keep these two sets of verbs straight: The verbs on the left all have the letter i as their first vowel. Remember that “the i-verbs indicate how I change my position.”
lines.465: Let’s take a look at the principal parts of these three pairs of verbs. Notice that the second verb in each pair is regular. You probably know these already:
lines.469: Perhaps the most difficult of all irregular verbs are lie and lay:
lines.478: I lay I laid I lied
lines.482: I have lain I have laid I have lied
lines.483: As you see here, there are two verbs to lie. One means to recline, and one means to fib. Lie (to fib) is easy—it’s a regular verb. Lay (to set down) is also a regular verb.
lines.485: Lie (to recline) is irregular, and it confuses many people because its past form, I lay, is identical to the present form of to lay (set down).
lines.486: To add to the confusion, in speech I lay down (the correct form) sounds exactly like I laid down (the wrong form), so we’re often making mistakes because we’re repeating the forms we hear—or think we hear. (The whole thing makes us want to lie down, no lie.)
lines.488: It is probably accurate to say that many English speakers, perhaps most of us, misuse lie sometimes, but you can master it in a few moments and remember it with a little review now and then.
lines.489: Even with irregular verbs, the past participle is always used with the auxiliary have (or its other forms has or had) to create perfect tenses (have lain). Forms of the verb be are always used with the -ing form (the present participle) to create progressive tenses.
